There's a New Single-Cylinder Norton Motorcycle in Town, 450 urban Literally Belongs on City Streets
18 photos
Photo: Norton
It's been six years or so since British bike maker Norton was brought back from the edge of the abyss by TVS Motor Company, and exactly one year since the crew announced its so-called Resurgence strategy. Time well spent, it seems, as the Brits have just announced they are entering a new segment with a brand-new bike.
At the Esposizione Internazionale Ciclo Motociclo e Accessori (EICMA) show in Milan, Italy, a new contender in the A2 category was unveiled. It's called the 450 urban (spelled exactly like that, with a lowercase "u"), and it targets the kind of riders who would usually not go for the likes of the Manx and Atlas.
Described as the father of a whole new generation of accessible urban exploration and commuting machines, the single-cylinder motorcycle has become the company's entry-level bike, but promises the same thrills as its bigger siblings.
Norton used an aluminum frame as a skeleton for the two-wheeler, and dressed it in a design that's at least in part inspired by the 1927 Norton CS1, a TT replica road bike that in some circles has a sort of cult following.
Neither naked nor fully faired, the urban kind of looks like many of the electric motorcycles that have popped up in recent years. One of the versions (there will be two of them) moves on 17-inch cast wheels painted in silver, the same color chosen for the frame, and are shod in road tires. The other uses black cast wheels and a grey frame.
Power for the rides comes from a liquid-cooled single-cylinder engine. True to the name the bike wears, it displaces 454cc, and it's only good for 46 horsepower at 8,000 rpm and 45 Nm of torque at 6,000 rpm, making it ideal for A2 license holders.
To aid people in the operation of the motorcycle, the engine is tied to a six-speed transmission with a quickshifter and draws its fuel from a three-gallon (12-liter) tank designed in a very angular fashion.
The suspension system the bike relies on is not some fancy setup capable of taking on rough trails, because that's not what the urban is all about. Instead, we're dealing with a fully adjustable 43 mm KYB upside-down fork at the front and a KYB rear monoshock that's adjustable for rebound and pre-load at the rear. ByBre hardware provides the stopping power.
Targeting a curb weight of 397 pounds (180 kg), the urban does not cut corners when it comes to extra fittings, so it'll ship to customers at an undisclosed point in the future with extended protective gear better suited for off-road motorcycles: mudguards, handguards, and fork protectors, among others.
Norton does not say how much it will charge for the 450 urban, or when we should expect it to get here. We'll keep an eye on things, though, and report back once we know more.
